name: Spanish conquest of the Aztec Empire
summary: In 1519 Hernán Cortés sailed from Cuba with a few hundred Spaniards, defying the governor who had cancelled his expedition. Landing on the Gulf coast, he won over the Totonacs of Cempoala, who resented Aztec tribute, and after a series of battles made an alliance with Tlaxcala, the Aztecs' unconquered enemy. In November 1519 Moctezuma II received him in Tenochtitlan, and Cortés soon held the emperor hostage. A massacre of Aztec nobles in May 1520 set off an uprising, and on La Noche Triste (30 June 1520) the Spaniards and their allies fled the city with heavy losses. Sheltered by Tlaxcala, Cortés rebuilt his forces while smallpox ravaged the Valley of Mexico and killed the new emperor, Cuitláhuac. From Texcoco, with thirteen brigantines and tens of thousands of Indigenous allies, he besieged Tenochtitlan from May 1521. The city fell on 13 August 1521, when Cuauhtémoc was captured, and New Spain was built on its ruins.
casualties: Estimates vary widely: about 1,800 Spaniards are estimated to have died over the whole campaign and many thousands of their Indigenous allies, while an estimated 100,000 to 240,000 Aztec warriors and civilians were killed, besides the far larger toll of the 1520 smallpox epidemic.

sides.name: Spain and its Indigenous allies (Tlaxcala, Totonacs, Texcoco and others)

events.label: 10 Feb 1519
events.text: Cortés's expedition leaves Cuba
events.detail: Two earlier Spanish voyages had touched the coasts of Yucatán and the Gulf of Mexico and heard of a rich empire inland. Diego Velázquez, governor of Cuba, chose Hernán Cortés to lead a third expedition, then cancelled his commission. Cortés sailed anyway in February 1519 with 11 ships carrying about 630 men, a few horses and some cannon, following the route of the first voyage along the Yucatán coast.

events.label: 24 Mar 1519
events.text: Potonchán makes peace and gives Cortés the interpreter Malintzin
events.detail: After defeating the Chontal Maya of Potonchán, on the Tabasco coast, in two battles, Cortés received their submission on 24 March 1519, with gifts that included twenty enslaved women. One of them, a Nahua woman the Spaniards called Doña Marina and the Nahuas Malintzin, spoke both Maya and Nahuatl. Working with Gerónimo de Aguilar, a shipwrecked Spaniard who spoke Maya, she let Cortés talk to the Aztecs, and she became his chief interpreter and adviser.

events.label: 22 Apr 1519
events.text: Cortés lands on the Gulf coast near San Juan de Ulúa
events.detail: The fleet anchored off San Juan de Ulúa, and the Spaniards came ashore on Good Friday, 22 April 1519. Envoys of the Aztec emperor Moctezuma II soon arrived with lavish gifts, and Cortés tried to impress them with a display of cannon fire and horses. The gifts were meant to persuade the strangers to leave, but they only convinced Cortés that great wealth lay inland.

events.label: Jun 1519
events.text: Veracruz is founded and the Totonacs of Cempoala ally with Cortés
events.detail: To escape the authority of Governor Velázquez, Cortés had his men found a town, La Villa Rica de la Vera Cruz, whose council named him its captain. At Cempoala, capital of the Totonacs, he persuaded the ruler Xicomecoatl to rebel against the Aztecs, and Moctezuma's tax collectors were seized. Cortés then sank his ships so that his men could not return to Cuba.

events.label: 2–5 Sep 1519
events.text: Battles with the Tlaxcalans
events.detail: Marching inland from 16 August with Totonac porters and warriors, the Spaniards entered the lands of Tlaxcala, a confederacy that had resisted the Aztecs for generations. Otomí and Tlaxcalan armies attacked them in a series of battles from 2 to 5 September 1519 and the fighting went on for days. Unable to destroy the Spaniards, and seeing them as enemies of Moctezuma, Tlaxcala's leaders chose to make peace.

events.label: 23 Sep 1519
events.text: Cortés enters Tlaxcala: the alliance that decided the war
events.detail: On 23 September 1519 Cortés entered the city of Tlaxcala, welcomed by its rulers Maxixcatzin and Xicotencatl the Elder, who saw the Spaniards as allies against the Aztecs. Tlaxcala had been encircled and blockaded by the empire for decades. Its warriors, porters and supplies, and its refuge after defeats, would make the conquest possible: tens of thousands of Tlaxcalans fought beside the Spaniards to the end.

events.label: 18 Oct 1519
events.text: The Cholula massacre
events.detail: Moctezuma's envoys steered Cortés through Cholula, a great sacred city that had broken with Tlaxcala to become an Aztec tributary. Claiming that the Cholulans planned an ambush, and urged on by his Tlaxcalan allies, Cortés had the city's nobles seized and killed in the main temple courtyard, and the city was sacked. Cortés reported about 3,000 dead and other witnesses far more; the massacre frightened other cities into negotiating.

events.label: 8 Nov 1519
events.text: Moctezuma receives Cortés in Tenochtitlan
events.detail: Crossing the mountains between the volcanoes, the Spaniards and their allies entered Tenochtitlan along the southern causeway on 8 November 1519. The island capital had an estimated 60,000 to more than 300,000 people, one of the largest cities in the world. Moctezuma met Cortés on the causeway and lodged the Spaniards in the palace of his father Axayacatl, at the heart of the city.

events.label: 14 Nov 1519
events.text: Cortés takes Moctezuma hostage
events.detail: After Aztec forces on the coast killed several Spaniards left at Veracruz, Cortés and his captains forced Moctezuma to move into the Spaniards' quarters, where he was held from 14 November 1519. The emperor kept ruling in name, under Cortés's control, and was made to swear allegiance to the Spanish king and hand over his treasure, while resentment grew among the Aztec nobility.

events.label: May 1520
events.text: Massacre at the Great Temple during the Toxcatl festival
events.detail: Cortés had left Pedro de Alvarado in charge of the small garrison in Tenochtitlan. During the festival of Toxcatl in May 1520, Alvarado, suspecting a plot, had his men close the temple courtyard and attack the unarmed nobles and dancers, killing many. The city rose in arms, and the Spaniards and their Tlaxcalan allies were besieged in their palace. Moctezuma, still a captive, was made to call for calm.

events.label: 27 May 1520
events.text: Cortés defeats Narváez at Cempoala
events.detail: Governor Velázquez sent Pánfilo de Narváez with some 900 Spaniards and 19 ships to arrest Cortés, and Narváez made Cempoala his base. Leaving Tenochtitlan with a few hundred men, Cortés attacked by night on 27 May 1520 with Chinantec allies, captured Narváez and won over most of his soldiers with promises of riches. Some of the newcomers carried smallpox, which then spread inland.

events.label: 30 Jun 1520
events.text: La Noche Triste: the Spaniards flee Tenochtitlan
events.detail: Cortés returned to the besieged palace on 24 June, but the city's nobles had chosen a new ruler, Cuitláhuac, and Moctezuma was killed in late June, by stones from his own people according to the Spaniards, by the Spaniards according to Aztec accounts. On the rainy night of 30 June 1520 Cortés broke out along the Tlacopan causeway. Hundreds of Spaniards and thousands of Tlaxcalans were killed, drowned or captured, and most of the treasure was lost.

events.label: 7 Jul 1520
events.text: Battle of Otumba
events.detail: The survivors retreated north around the lakes, harassed all the way. On 7 July 1520, on the plain near Otumba, a large Aztec army blocked their road to Tlaxcala. Cortés and his horsemen charged the Aztec commander, the cihuacoatl Matlatzincatl, and killed him, and the Aztec army broke off. Days later the exhausted, mostly wounded Spaniards reached Tlaxcala, whose rulers refused Aztec offers and kept the alliance.

events.label: Aug 1520
events.text: The Tepeaca campaign
events.detail: To rebuild his reputation and secure the roads to the coast, Cortés led Spaniards and Tlaxcalans against Tepeaca, an Aztec tributary whose people had killed Spaniards, from early August 1520. Tepeaca was defeated and became an allied town. Other tributary towns, seeing the Aztecs unable to protect them, began to change sides, while Cortés received reinforcements from ships arriving on the coast.

events.label: 4 Dec 1520
events.text: Smallpox kills the emperor Cuitláhuac
events.detail: Smallpox, unknown in the Americas, spread through the Valley of Mexico from the autumn of 1520 for about seventy days. Many thousands died, and others starved because no one was well enough to feed them. The emperor Cuitláhuac died on 4 December 1520, after ruling for eighty days; he was succeeded early in 1521 by Cuauhtémoc. The epidemic also struck Tlaxcala, killing the ruler Maxixcatzin.

events.label: 26 Dec 1520
events.text: Cortés marches on Texcoco, which becomes his base
events.detail: On the day after Christmas 1520 Cortés left Tlaxcala with his Spaniards and more than 10,000 Tlaxcalan warriors under Chichimecatecuhtli, and crossed into the Valley of Mexico. At Texcoco, once the Aztecs' partner in the Triple Alliance, he installed a friendly ruler, Ixtlilxochitl II. Texcoco, on the eastern shore of the lake, became the base from which the siege of Tenochtitlan was prepared.

events.label: Apr 1521
events.text: Cortés circles the lakes and fights at Xochimilco
events.detail: Having won over Chalco and Tlalmanalco and beaten Aztec forces around Chalco in March 1521, Cortés set out in April with some 20,000 allied warriors on a circuit of the southern and western lakeshore. He fought a hard battle at Xochimilco, Tenochtitlan's ally, then found Coyoacán, Tlacopan and Azcapotzalco deserted, and returned to Texcoco, where thirteen brigantines built from Tlaxcalan timber were nearly ready.

events.label: 26 May 1521
events.text: The siege of Tenochtitlan begins
events.detail: Three columns, each of about 200 Spaniards and 8,000 Indigenous warriors, took up positions on the lakeshore at Tlacopan under Pedro de Alvarado, Coyoacán under Cristóbal de Olid and Iztapalapa under Gonzalo de Sandoval. Alvarado and Olid cut the aqueduct from Chapultepec that carried the city's fresh water. Cortés launched the thirteen brigantines, which scattered the Aztec canoes and took control of the lake.

events.label: 30 Jun 1521
events.text: Aztec victory on the causeway: Spanish prisoners sacrificed
events.detail: Cortés ordered a combined push into the city towards the great market of Tlatelolco but failed to fill in a breach behind his men. The Aztecs counter-attacked, Cortés was wounded and nearly captured, and dozens of Spaniards were taken alive and sacrificed at the Great Temple in sight of their comrades. Many allies briefly left the besiegers, but the blockade held and famine spread in the city.

events.label: 1 Aug 1521
events.text: The besiegers reach the marketplace of Tlatelolco
events.detail: Advancing street by street along the causeways, the Spaniards and their allies razed each district they took and used the rubble to fill the canals. By the start of August they had broken into the market square of Tlatelolco, in the north of the island, where Alvarado's men set fire to the temple. The defenders, starving and drinking brackish water, were penned into the last corner of the city.

events.label: 13 Aug 1521
events.text: Tenochtitlan falls and Cuauhtémoc is captured
events.detail: On 13 August 1521 Cuauhtémoc tried to escape across the lake by canoe and was captured by one of Sandoval's brigantines, and the last defenders surrendered. Tens of thousands had died in the siege, and allied warriors killed many of the survivors. The Aztec Empire ended; its tributary cities passed under Spanish rule, and Mexico City, capital of New Spain, was built on the ruins.

name: Spanish American Wars of Independence (South America)
summary: Napoleon's capture of Spain's king in 1808 left Spanish America without a legitimate government, and in 1810 juntas took power in Caracas, Buenos Aires, Bogotá and Santiago, setting off wars between patriots and royalists across South America. In the north, Simón Bolívar lost two Venezuelan republics, in 1812 and 1814, and Spain's expedition under Pablo Morillo reconquered New Granada in 1815–16. From a base on the Orinoco, Bolívar crossed the Andes and won at Boyacá in 1819, joined Venezuela and New Granada into Gran Colombia, and won Venezuela at Carabobo in 1821. In the south, José de San Martín crossed the Andes from Argentina, freed Chile at Chacabuco and Maipú, and took Lima in 1821. After the two liberators met at Guayaquil in 1822, Bolívar and Antonio José de Sucre finished the war in Peru at Junín and Ayacucho in 1824. Bolivia was founded in 1825, and the last royalist fortress, Callao, surrendered in January 1826.
casualties: No reliable total exists; one estimate quoted for all of Spanish America from Mexico to Argentina is about 1,000,000 deaths, some 400,000 of them in New Granada and Venezuela, many from disease, hunger and massacres rather than battle.

events.label: 19 Apr 1810
events.text: Caracas deposes its captain general and forms a junta
events.detail: Napoleon had forced Spain's king, Ferdinand VII, to abdicate in 1808, and by 1810 French armies had cornered Spain's resistance government in Cádiz. When news reached Caracas, the town council met on 19 April 1810 and deposed Captain General Vicente Emparan. It set up a Supreme Junta that claimed to rule in Ferdinand's name. Juntas soon followed across Spanish America, and civil war broke out between their supporters and royalists loyal to the government in Spain.

events.label: 25 May 1810
events.text: The May Revolution in Buenos Aires
events.detail: In Buenos Aires, capital of the Viceroyalty of the Río de la Plata, an open town meeting removed the viceroy and on 25 May 1810 installed a governing junta. Córdoba, Montevideo, Paraguay and Upper Peru resisted it, and Buenos Aires sent armies against them. The new government never fell to Spain again, and its region became the base of the southern war against the royalists.

events.label: 5 Jul 1811
events.text: Venezuela declares independence
events.detail: Pushed by Francisco de Miranda and the young radicals of the Patriotic Society, the Venezuelan congress voted on 5 July 1811 to declare independence, the first Spanish American colony to do so. Seven of the ten provinces of the old captaincy general joined the new confederation. Maracaibo, Guayana and the district of Coro stayed loyal to Spain, and an expedition to bring Coro under the republic failed.

events.label: 26 Mar 1812
events.text: An earthquake devastates republican Venezuela
events.detail: On Maundy Thursday, 26 March 1812, a powerful earthquake struck Venezuela. It did most of its damage in republican towns such as Caracas, while royalist areas were largely spared, and some clergy preached that it was God's punishment for rebellion. The disaster came just as the Spanish naval captain Domingo de Monteverde was advancing from Coro, and it helped turn many people against the young republic.

events.label: 25 Jul 1812
events.text: Miranda surrenders at San Mateo: the First Republic falls
events.detail: Monteverde's small force grew as it marched from Coro, entering Valencia on 3 May 1812. On 30 June royalist prisoners seized the castle of Puerto Cabello, with its ammunition, from its commander Simón Bolívar. Believing the cause lost, Miranda signed a capitulation with Monteverde at San Mateo on 25 July, and royalist troops entered Caracas on 1 August. Bolívar escaped to Curaçao; Miranda was handed to the Spanish and died in a Cádiz prison.

events.label: 15 Dec 1812
events.text: Bolívar's Cartagena Manifesto
events.detail: From exile, Bolívar went to Cartagena, which had declared itself an independent republic. On 15 December 1812 he published his Cartagena Manifesto, blaming the fall of Venezuela on its weak federal government, divisions among republicans and the effects of the earthquake. He warned New Granada that royalist Venezuela threatened it too, and asked its leaders to back a campaign to retake Caracas. He then cleared royalists from the Magdalena River.

events.label: 15 Jun 1813
events.text: Bolívar declares 'war to the death' at Trujillo
events.detail: With New Granada's approval, Bolívar crossed into Venezuela in May 1813 in what became the Admirable Campaign. At Trujillo on 15 June he issued his Decree of War to the Death: Spaniards and Canary Islanders who did not actively support independence would be killed, while American-born people would be spared even if they had served the royalists. He meant to divide Venezuelans from Spaniards. Both sides went on to kill prisoners on a terrible scale.

events.label: 6 Aug 1813
events.text: Bolívar enters Caracas at the end of the Admirable Campaign
events.detail: Bolívar's small army won a string of battles across the Andes and the western plains, while Santiago Mariño freed the east from a base in Cumaná. The royalist government surrendered on 4 August, and Bolívar entered Caracas in triumph on 6 August 1813, besieging Monteverde in Puerto Cabello. He restored the republic, now called the Second Republic, under his own military rule, and was hailed as the Liberator.

events.label: 15 Jun 1814
events.text: Boves crushes the republicans at La Puerta
events.detail: The Second Republic never won over the poor. José Tomás Boves, a Spanish-born trader turned royalist chieftain, raised an army of llaneros, the mixed-race cowboys of the plains, promising them the property of the rich. After several defeats he routed Bolívar and Mariño at La Puerta on 15 June 1814. He took Valencia and Caracas in July, and thousands of people fled east with Bolívar in a terrible exodus.

events.label: 2 Oct 1814
events.text: Royalists destroy the Chilean patriots at Rancagua
events.detail: Chile had set up its own junta in September 1810. In 1814 the viceroy of Peru sent an army under Mariano Osorio to crush it. Divided between Bernardo O'Higgins and José Miguel Carrera, the patriots made their stand in the town of Rancagua on 1–2 October and were overwhelmed. Chile returned to royalist rule, and O'Higgins and many others fled across the Andes to Mendoza.

events.label: 5 Dec 1814
events.text: Boves is killed at Urica as the Second Republic ends
events.detail: In the east the republicans made a last stand. At Urica on 5 December 1814 Boves's army beat them again, though Boves himself was killed by a lance. His lieutenant Francisco Tomás Morales finished the campaign, capturing and executing José Félix Ribas and taking the last republican town, Maturín. By the end of 1814 Venezuela was royalist again, and Bolívar had gone to serve New Granada.

events.label: Sep 1815
events.text: Bolívar writes the Jamaica Letter
events.detail: Bolívar left New Granada for Jamaica in May 1815, defeated and without resources. In Kingston, in September 1815, he wrote a long letter to a British gentleman, now called the Jamaica Letter. It explained why Spanish Americans were justified in seeking independence, called on Europe to help, and sketched the future of the new nations, which he thought should be republics with strong governments. It became one of the founding texts of Latin American independence.

events.label: 6 Dec 1815
events.text: Cartagena falls to Morillo after a 105-day siege
events.detail: With Napoleon defeated, Ferdinand VII sent General Pablo Morillo to America with about 10,000 men, the largest expedition Spain had ever sent there. After securing Venezuela, Morillo besieged Cartagena from 26 August 1815. Cut off by land and sea, the city starved; thousands of its people died of hunger and disease before it surrendered on 6 December. Morillo's army then pushed into the interior of New Granada.

events.label: 6 May 1816
events.text: Royalists take Bogotá and end New Granada's republic
events.detail: While Morillo marched south from the coast, a second royalist column under Sebastián de la Calzada invaded from the Venezuelan plains, won at Cachirí in February 1816 and entered Bogotá on 6 May. The last republican forces were beaten at Cuchilla del Tambo in June. Morillo's courts executed many of the republic's leaders, and some 7,000 people are estimated to have been executed between 1816 and 1819.

events.label: 12 Feb 1817
events.text: San Martín crosses the Andes and wins at Chacabuco
events.detail: José de San Martín spent two years building the Army of the Andes at Mendoza. From 19 January 1817 about 4,000 men crossed the mountains in columns by passes averaging some 3,000 metres high, a march of about three weeks. On 12 February they beat the royalists at Chacabuco, north of Santiago, and entered the capital. San Martín declined to rule Chile, and O'Higgins became its Supreme Director.

events.label: 17 Jul 1817
events.text: Patriots take Angostura on the Orinoco
events.detail: Back from Haiti, where President Alexandre Pétion had armed him in exchange for a promise to free the slaves, Bolívar joined Manuel Piar in Guayana. Piar beat the royalists at San Félix in April, and on 17 July 1817 the starving garrison of Angostura abandoned the city by river. Angostura gave the patriots a capital, a port open to foreign trade and a route up the Orinoco to the plains held by José Antonio Páez.

events.label: 5 Apr 1818
events.text: Maipú secures Chile's independence
events.detail: Chile declared independence on 12 February 1818, but a new royalist army under Osorio landed in the south and surprised the patriots at night at Cancha Rayada on 19 March. San Martín rallied his scattered army near Santiago, and on 5 April 1818 he crushed Osorio on the plains of Maipú. The royalists never threatened Santiago again, and Chile became the base for an attack on Peru.

events.label: 15 Feb 1819
events.text: The Congress of Angostura opens
events.detail: Bolívar called a congress of delegates from the patriot-held parts of Venezuela, with a few exiles from New Granada. It opened at Angostura on 15 February 1819, where Bolívar gave a famous address calling for a strong central government and equality among races. The congress elected him president. It went on to proclaim, in December, the union of Venezuela and New Granada.

events.label: 6 Jul 1819
events.text: Bolívar's army crosses the Andes by the Páramo de Pisba
events.detail: Instead of attacking Morillo in Venezuela, Bolívar struck at New Granada in the rainy season, when no one expected it. He marched from the Apure across flooded plains, met Francisco de Paula Santander at Tame on 11 June and began climbing the Eastern Andes on 22 June. On the bleak Páramo de Pisba many soldiers died of cold and most of the horses were lost, but on 6 July the army came down into New Granada.

events.label: 7 Aug 1819
events.text: Bolívar wins at Boyacá and takes Bogotá
events.detail: After a hard fight at Vargas Swamp on 25 July, Bolívar slipped round the royalist army of José María Barreiro and reached Tunja first. On 7 August 1819, as Barreiro hurried to protect Bogotá, Bolívar caught his army crossing the bridge at Boyacá and forced most of it to surrender. The viceroy fled, and Bolívar entered Bogotá on 10 August. New Granada became the base for the rest of his campaigns.

events.label: 17 Dec 1819
events.text: The Congress of Angostura proclaims the Republic of Colombia
events.detail: On 17 December 1819 the congress at Angostura passed a Fundamental Law joining Venezuela and New Granada into a single Republic of Colombia, which historians call Gran Colombia to tell it apart from today's Colombia. Quito was to join once freed. Bolívar was its president. The union was confirmed by the Congress of Cúcuta, which adopted a constitution on 30 August 1821.

events.label: 8 Sep 1820
events.text: San Martín's Liberating Expedition lands in Peru
events.detail: Peru was the centre of royal power in South America. San Martín's expedition of about 4,000 soldiers, most of them Chileans, sailed from Valparaíso on 20 August 1820 escorted by Lord Cochrane's fleet. It landed at Paracas Bay near Pisco on 8 September. San Martín preferred to win Peruvians over rather than fight, while Juan Antonio Álvarez de Arenales led a column through the highlands and Trujillo declared for independence in December.

events.label: 24 Jun 1821
events.text: Bolívar and Páez win the Battle of Carabobo
events.detail: A liberal revolution in Spain in 1820 stopped reinforcements for Morillo, who agreed a truce with Bolívar in November and went home. The war resumed in April 1821 after Maracaibo joined Colombia. Bolívar marched from New Granada with about 7,000 men and, with Páez's plainsmen and the British Legion, routed Miguel de la Torre at Carabobo on 24 June 1821. He entered Caracas on 29 June; Venezuela was effectively free.

events.label: 28 Jul 1821
events.text: San Martín proclaims the independence of Peru in Lima
events.detail: As patriot guerrillas closed in and the north of the country went over to independence, the new viceroy, José de la Serna, abandoned Lima and withdrew his army to the highlands, leaving a garrison in the fortress of Callao. San Martín entered the city, became Protector of Peru and proclaimed its independence on 28 July 1821. Callao surrendered in September, but the royalist army remained strong in the Andes.

events.label: 24 May 1822
events.text: Sucre wins the Battle of Pichincha and frees Quito
events.detail: Guayaquil had declared independence in October 1820, and Bolívar sent Antonio José de Sucre to take Quito. After two failed advances, Sucre marched south through Cuenca and then north up the Andes, joined by Peruvian and Argentine troops sent by San Martín. On 24 May 1822 his men climbed the slopes of the Pichincha volcano above Quito and beat the royalists. Quito surrendered the next day, and Pasto gave up in June.

events.label: 26 Jul 1822
events.text: Bolívar and San Martín meet at Guayaquil
events.detail: On 26 and 27 July 1822 the two liberators met in private at Guayaquil, which Bolívar had just annexed to Colombia. No record was kept. San Martín seems to have asked for troops and even offered to serve under Bolívar, but they disagreed over how the new states should be governed. Soon afterwards San Martín resigned his command in Peru and left for Chile, Argentina and finally France, leaving the war to Bolívar.

events.label: 6 Aug 1824
events.text: Bolívar's cavalry wins at Junín
events.detail: Royalist armies retook Lima twice, in June 1823 and in February 1824, after the patriot garrison of Callao mutinied and handed the fortress to Spain. Named dictator by Peru's congress, Bolívar rebuilt his army at Trujillo and marched south over the Andes. On the high plain of Junín on 6 August 1824 his cavalry met José de Canterac's horsemen in a battle of lances and sabres, and the royalists fell back towards Cuzco.

events.label: 9 Dec 1824
events.text: Sucre's victory at Ayacucho ends Spain's main army
events.detail: Viceroy la Serna advanced with a larger army against Sucre, who chose to fight on the plain of Ayacucho near Quinua on 9 December 1824. In a few hours the patriots, about 6,000 Colombians, Peruvians and others, broke the royalist attack and captured the viceroy. His generals signed a capitulation surrendering the Royal Army of Peru. The battle effectively secured the independence of Peru and of Spanish South America.

events.label: 6 Aug 1825
events.text: Upper Peru declares its independence as Bolivia
events.detail: The royalist general Pedro Antonio de Olañeta refused to accept Ayacucho and held Upper Peru. Sucre entered it on 25 February 1825 as royalist units deserted or changed sides, and Olañeta was mortally wounded at Tumusla on 1 April. An assembly met at Chuquisaca and on 6 August 1825 declared Upper Peru an independent republic, named after Bolívar. Sucre became its first president.

events.label: 23 Jan 1826
events.text: Callao surrenders, ending Spanish rule in South America
events.detail: In the fortress of Callao, the Spanish brigadier José Ramón Rodil refused to recognise the surrender at Ayacucho and held out, hoping for help from Spain. About 8,000 refugees crowded in with his garrison, and thousands died of hunger and disease as the siege dragged on. With food and ammunition gone and no help coming, Rodil negotiated and handed over the fortress on 23 January 1826, the last Spanish stronghold on the South American mainland.

name: War of 1812
summary: While Britain fought Napoleon, its blockade of France and the impressment of seamen from American ships angered the United States, and Americans blamed Britain for backing Indigenous resistance in the Old Northwest, where the Shawnee leader Tecumseh had built a confederacy of nations. Some Americans also hoped to annex Canada. Congress declared war in June 1812, but invasions of Upper and Lower Canada failed, and in August 1812 an American army surrendered Detroit to British troops and Tecumseh's warriors. In 1813 Oliver Hazard Perry won control of Lake Erie and Tecumseh was killed at the Thames, while in the south the Creek War ended in 1814 with heavy Creek land cessions. After Napoleon's defeat in 1814 Britain went on the offensive, burning Washington, but it was repulsed at Baltimore and Plattsburgh. The Treaty of Ghent, signed in December 1814, restored the prewar borders. Andrew Jackson's victory at New Orleans came weeks later, before news of the peace arrived. Canada stayed British, while Indigenous nations lost most of their remaining lands south of the Great Lakes.
casualties: An estimated 15,000 Americans died from all causes, about 2,200 of them in battle; British and Canadian deaths are estimated at up to about 10,000, and Indigenous nations lost an estimated 10,000 warriors and civilians, many from disease.

sides.name: Britain, its North American colonies and Indigenous allies

events.label: 18 Jun 1812
events.text: The United States declares war on Britain
events.detail: British orders in council restricting neutral trade with France, the impressment of seamen from American ships and British support for Indigenous resistance in the Northwest had soured relations for years. On 1 June President James Madison asked Congress for war. The House voted 79 to 49 and the Senate 19 to 13, and Madison signed the declaration on 18 June. Opposition was strongest among Federalists in New England, whose trade depended on peace with Britain.

events.label: 17 Jul 1812
events.text: British and Indigenous force takes Fort Mackinac without a fight
events.detail: On Brock's orders, Captain Charles Roberts set out from Fort St. Joseph with British soldiers, fur traders and voyageurs and Ojibwe, Odawa, Menominee, Ho-Chunk and Sioux warriors. They landed on Mackinac Island and hauled a cannon onto the heights above the fort. Its commander, who had not yet heard that war had been declared, surrendered on 17 July. The easy success drew more Indigenous nations to the British side.

events.label: 16 Aug 1812
events.text: Hull surrenders Detroit to Brock and Tecumseh
events.detail: General William Hull invaded Upper Canada from Detroit on 12 July, but with his supply line threatened by Tecumseh's warriors he retreated to Detroit. Isaac Brock crossed the river with British troops, Canadian militia and Tecumseh's fighters and warned that his Indigenous allies might be beyond his control in an assault. Hull surrendered on 16 August with more than 2,000 men. The defeat left the British in control of Michigan Territory for more than a year.

events.label: 19 Aug 1812
events.text: USS Constitution defeats HMS Guerriere
events.detail: About 400 miles south-east of Halifax, the American frigate Constitution under Isaac Hull met the British frigate Guerriere under James Dacres. In a short, close action Guerriere's masts were shot away, and she was so badly damaged that her captors set her on fire. The British lost 15 killed and 78 wounded, the Americans 7 killed. Though of little military weight for the Royal Navy, the victory lifted American spirits days after Detroit fell.

events.label: 13 Oct 1812
events.text: Battle of Queenston Heights: Brock killed as an invasion fails
events.detail: American troops under Stephen Van Rensselaer crossed the Niagara River and seized the heights above Queenston. Brock was killed leading a counterattack early in the fighting. Roger Sheaffe then brought up British regulars, militia and Mohawk warriors under John Norton, while many New York militiamen refused to cross the river to reinforce their comrades. The Americans on the heights, among them Winfield Scott, surrendered; about 955 were taken prisoner.

events.label: 22 Jan 1813
events.text: Battle of Frenchtown on the River Raisin
events.detail: An American force under James Winchester, advancing towards Detroit in midwinter, occupied Frenchtown on the River Raisin. On 22 January British troops and Indigenous warriors under Henry Procter attacked and forced it to surrender. Wounded American prisoners left behind were killed the next day, about 60 by some accounts. The killings became a rallying cry in Kentucky and the West and hardened American resolve to retake Detroit.

events.label: 27 Apr 1813
events.text: Americans capture and burn York, capital of Upper Canada
events.detail: Using their new squadron on Lake Ontario, American forces landed near York and drove off the outnumbered British regulars, who blew up their powder magazine as they withdrew, killing and wounding many attackers, among them General Zebulon Pike. During an occupation of nearly two weeks American troops burned the legislative buildings and other public property. The raid gained little militarily, but the British later cited it when they burned Washington in 1814.

events.label: 27 May 1813
events.text: Americans take Fort George, but are checked on the Niagara
events.detail: After a two-day bombardment, American troops stormed ashore at the mouth of the Niagara River on 27 May and captured Fort George. The retreating British struck back: a night attack at Stoney Creek on 5 June drove the American advance back, and on 24 June an American column surrendered at Beaver Dams to a smaller British and Indigenous force. The Americans were left holding little beyond Fort George itself.

events.label: 30 Aug 1813
events.text: Red Stick Creeks storm Fort Mims, widening the war in the south
events.detail: In summer 1813 a civil war split the Creek Nation between the Red Sticks, who opposed land cessions and American ways, and Creeks who favoured accommodation. After American militia ambushed a Red Stick supply train at Burnt Corn in July, Red Stick warriors under Peter McQueen and William Weatherford stormed Fort Mims, a stockade about 35 miles north of Mobile, on 30 August. Most of the 500 or so militia, settlers and mixed-race Creek families inside were killed, and the Creek civil war became a war with the United States.

events.label: 10 Sep 1813
events.text: Battle of Lake Erie: Perry captures the British squadron
events.detail: Both sides raced to build warships on Lake Erie. Near Put-in-Bay, Oliver Hazard Perry's squadron engaged Robert Barclay's. When Perry's flagship Lawrence was battered into surrender he crossed in a small boat to the Niagara and led a renewed attack, and all six British vessels struck their colours. 'We have met the enemy and they are ours,' Perry reported. Control of the lake cut the supply line of the British army at Detroit.

events.label: 5 Oct 1813
events.text: Battle of the Thames: Tecumseh is killed
events.detail: Without supplies by water, Henry Procter abandoned Detroit and Amherstburg and retreated up the Thames River, against Tecumseh's protests. William Henry Harrison's army of some 3,000 caught his roughly 950 British troops and Indigenous warriors near Moraviantown on 5 October. Richard Johnson's mounted infantry broke the British line, and Tecumseh was killed, after which his warriors withdrew. His death broke up the confederacy, and the United States regained Detroit and Michigan Territory.

events.label: 11 Nov 1813
events.text: Battle of Crysler's Farm ends the campaign against Montreal
events.detail: In autumn 1813 two American armies advanced on Montreal. In late October Charles de Salaberry's small force of Canadian Voltigeurs, militia and Mohawk warriors turned back Wade Hampton's 4,000 men at the Châteauguay River. On 11 November, at Crysler's Farm on the St. Lawrence, about 800 British and Canadian troops under Joseph Morrison defeated James Wilkinson's rearguard of some 2,500. Both American armies withdrew into winter quarters, and Lower Canada was safe.

events.label: 30 Dec 1813
events.text: British and Indigenous forces burn Buffalo
events.detail: Abandoning Fort George in December, American militia burned the Canadian town of Newark on 10 December, leaving its people homeless in winter. The British retaliated across the Niagara frontier: they took Fort Niagara, raided and burned Lewiston, where civilians were killed, and on 30 December attacked and burned Buffalo and Black Rock. The cycle of reprisals left both banks of the Niagara devastated by the end of the year.

events.label: 27 Mar 1814
events.text: Battle of Horseshoe Bend breaks the Red Stick Creeks
events.detail: Andrew Jackson's Tennessee militia, US regulars and Cherokee and Creek allies attacked about 1,000 Red Sticks fortified in a bend of the Tallapoosa River. Some 800 Red Sticks were killed, against 49 of Jackson's men killed and 154 wounded. In the Treaty of Fort Jackson that August, Jackson forced the Creek Nation, including the Creeks who had fought beside him, to give up about 23 million acres, roughly half its land.

events.label: 31 May 1814
events.text: Britain extends its blockade to the whole American coast
events.detail: The Royal Navy had declared Chesapeake and Delaware Bays under blockade in December 1812. With Napoleon defeated and abdicated in April 1814, Britain sent more ships and veteran troops across the Atlantic, and on 31 May it extended the blockade to the entire coast. American exports, worth $130 million in 1807, fell to about $7 million in 1814, and customs revenue, the government's main income, fell by more than half.

events.label: 25 Jul 1814
events.text: Battle of Lundy's Lane, the war's bloodiest battle
events.detail: Jacob Brown's American army crossed the Niagara River, took Fort Erie on 3 July and defeated a British force at Chippawa on 5 July. On 25 July it met the British again at Lundy's Lane, close to Niagara Falls, in a battle that raged into the night and became the costliest of the war. Neither side could claim victory, but the Americans fell back to Fort Erie, where they beat off a British assault in August.

events.label: 24 Aug 1814
events.text: British troops defeat the Americans at Bladensburg and burn Washington
events.detail: A British force of about 4,500 under Robert Ross, guided by Rear Admiral George Cockburn, landed in Maryland and routed American militia at Bladensburg on 24 August. That evening the troops entered Washington and set fire to the Capitol, with the Library of Congress inside it, the President's House, the Treasury and the War Department. President Madison fled. The British, citing the burning of York, left after about a day.

events.label: Sep 1814
events.text: British forces occupy eastern Maine
events.detail: Britain hoped to gain a land route between Halifax and Quebec in any peace. Its forces took Moose Island at Eastport in July, and in September John Sherbrooke led some 3,000 troops from Halifax up the Penobscot River, capturing Castine and destroying or seizing 17 American ships in a campaign of 26 days. The coast of Maine east of the Penobscot was held for the rest of the war and returned under the peace treaty.

events.label: 11 Sep 1814
events.text: Battle of Plattsburgh: invasion from Canada turned back
events.detail: George Prevost marched south from Canada along Lake Champlain with more than 8,000 troops. On 11 September Thomas Macdonough's American squadron, anchored in Plattsburgh Bay, defeated and captured the British flotilla, whose commander George Downie was killed. Without control of the lake to supply his army, Prevost called off the land attack and withdrew, weakening Britain's hand at the peace talks.

events.label: 12–14 Sep 1814
events.text: Baltimore holds: Fort McHenry withstands bombardment
events.detail: About 5,000 British troops landed at North Point to attack Baltimore. On 12 September American militia delayed them, and Robert Ross was killed by a sharpshooter. On 13 and 14 September British ships bombarded Fort McHenry for about 25 hours, but its garrison held, and the British withdrew. Seeing the flag still flying at dawn, the lawyer Francis Scott Key wrote the verses that became 'The Star-Spangled Banner'.

events.label: 24 Dec 1814
events.text: Treaty of Ghent signed
events.detail: Peace talks had begun at Ghent in August 1814, with Britain at first demanding territory and an Indigenous buffer state. The British failures at Plattsburgh and Baltimore removed the case for territorial gains, and both sides settled for the prewar status quo. Signed on 24 December, the treaty returned captured territory, set up commissions for disputed boundaries and promised to restore Indigenous nations' rights of 1811, but it said nothing about impressment or neutral rights.

events.label: 8 Jan 1815
events.text: Battle of New Orleans: Jackson repulses the British
events.detail: A British expedition under Edward Pakenham landed below New Orleans in December. On 8 January about 8,000 British troops assaulted Andrew Jackson's earthworks at Chalmette, defended by some 5,700 regulars, militia and volunteers. The attack failed within hours: the British lost about 2,000 killed, wounded or captured, Pakenham among the dead, while the Americans lost 71. The battle came after the treaty was signed but before word reached America.

events.label: 16–17 Feb 1815
events.text: The United States ratifies the peace and the war ends
events.detail: News of the treaty reached Washington in February, just after news of New Orleans and as Federalist delegates from the Hartford Convention arrived with New England's complaints about the war. The Senate approved the treaty on 16 February and ratifications were exchanged on 17 February, ending the war. On the Gulf Coast the British had taken Fort Bowyer on 12 February, but word of peace halted their attack on Mobile.

name: Texas Revolution
summary: In the early 1830s Mexico's government tried to slow the flood of settlers from the United States into Texas, then part of the state of Coahuila y Texas: a law of 1830 banned further American immigration and new imports of enslaved people. When Antonio López de Santa Anna abandoned the federal Constitution of 1824 and concentrated power in Mexico City, Anglo-American settlers and many Tejanos rose in revolt. Fighting began at Gonzales on 2 October 1835, and by December Texian volunteers had driven the last Mexican garrison out of San Antonio de Béxar. Early in 1836 Santa Anna led an army north. His troops stormed the Alamo on 6 March, while General José de Urrea swept up the coast and some 350 Texian prisoners were executed at Goliad. A convention declared independence on 2 March. Sam Houston's army retreated east, then routed Santa Anna at San Jacinto on 21 April 1836 and captured him the next day. The Treaties of Velasco promised a Mexican withdrawal, but Mexico refused to recognise the Republic of Texas.
casualties: An estimated 600 Texian and 1,000 Mexican soldiers died in the fighting and executions of 1835–36, with about 350 Texians and 400 Mexicans wounded and some 700 Mexican soldiers captured.

sides.name: Texian and Tejano rebels (Republic of Texas from 2 March 1836)

events.label: 2 Oct 1835
events.text: Battle of Gonzales: the first shots of the revolution
events.detail: Tension had been rising as Santa Anna's government turned against federalism, and in September 1835 General Martín Perfecto de Cos landed at Copano with about 500 soldiers. Troops from San Antonio de Béxar were sent to take back a small cannon lent to the settlers of Gonzales for defence. The settlers refused to give it up, and on 2 October 1835 Texian volunteers attacked Lieutenant Francisco de Castañeda's dragoons, who withdrew to Béxar after a brief skirmish. The clash began open war.

events.label: 10 Oct 1835
events.text: Texian volunteers capture the presidio at Goliad
events.detail: Presidio La Bahía at Goliad guarded the road between the coast and San Antonio and held supplies the Mexican army needed. On 10 October 1835 about 125 Texian volunteers under George Collingsworth stormed it and took the small garrison after a fight of about half an hour. The loss cut Cos off from the port of Copano. The next day the volunteers gathered at Gonzales elected Stephen F. Austin to command their army, which then marched on San Antonio.

events.label: 28 Oct 1835
events.text: Battle of Concepción outside San Antonio
events.detail: As the Texian army advanced on San Antonio de Béxar, where Cos had gathered his troops, about 90 men under James Bowie and James Fannin camped by Mission Concepción. On 28 October 1835 Colonel Domingo Ugartechea attacked them with about 275 infantry and cavalry and two cannon. Sheltered along a riverbank, the Texians beat back the attacks and lost one man killed, while Mexican dead are estimated at 14 to 76. The Texians then settled down to besiege Béxar.

events.label: 3 Nov 1835
events.text: The Consultation meets at San Felipe and names Sam Houston to command
events.detail: Delegates from the Texas settlements met at San Felipe de Austin on 3 November 1835 to decide what they were fighting for. Most still hoped to restore Mexico's federal Constitution of 1824 rather than break away. The Consultation set up a provisional government with a governor and a council, created a regular army and on 13 November named Sam Houston its commander-in-chief. Quarrels between governor and council soon left Texas with weak and divided leadership.

events.label: 26 Nov 1835
events.text: The Grass Fight outside Béxar
events.detail: During the siege of Béxar, Texian scouts reported a Mexican pack train approaching the town on 26 November 1835, and many believed it carried silver to pay Cos's troops. Edward Burleson's men attacked and drove the escort back into the town, killing an estimated 50 Mexican soldiers for two Texians wounded. The mules turned out to be carrying fodder for the garrison's horses, and the skirmish became known as the Grass Fight. The siege dragged on into December.

events.label: 5–10 Dec 1835
events.text: Texians storm San Antonio de Béxar and Cos surrenders
events.detail: After weeks of siege, Ben Milam and Frank Johnson led volunteers into San Antonio de Béxar on 5 December 1835, fighting from house to house for four days; Milam was killed on 7 December. On 9 December Cos withdrew into the Alamo mission and asked for terms, agreed early on 10 December. His men pledged not to oppose the Constitution of 1824, and Cos left Béxar on 14 December with about 800 soldiers, leaving no Mexican garrison in Texas.

events.label: 30 Dec 1835
events.text: Mexico decrees that armed foreign volunteers will be treated as pirates
events.detail: Many volunteers had arrived from the United States, among them the New Orleans Greys, and Mexico's government believed the revolt was being fed from across the border. At Santa Anna's urging, a decree issued in late December 1835 and known after the war minister José María Tornel declared that armed foreigners taken fighting Mexican troops would be treated as pirates and could be executed. It would be invoked to justify the killing of prisoners in the spring of 1836.

events.label: Feb 1836
events.text: Santa Anna's army crosses the Rio Grande into Texas
events.detail: Determined to crush the revolt himself, Santa Anna gathered an army of several thousand men at Saltillo and marched it north through a harsh winter. His main force crossed the Rio Grande in mid-February 1836 and made for San Antonio, while General José de Urrea led a second column up the coast from Matamoros. The Texians were poorly prepared: their government was paralysed by quarrels, and many volunteers had gone off to join a planned expedition against Matamoros.

events.label: 23 Feb 1836
events.text: Siege of the Alamo begins
events.detail: On 23 February 1836 about 1,500 Mexican soldiers entered San Antonio de Béxar, and the town's small Texian garrison under William B. Travis and James Bowie fell back into the fortified Alamo mission. On 24 February Travis wrote his famous appeal 'To the People of Texas & All Americans in the World', pledging to hold out and asking for reinforcements. Few came. Mexican artillery bombarded the walls while more of Santa Anna's troops arrived, and the siege lasted thirteen days.

events.label: 27 Feb – 2 Mar 1836
events.text: Urrea routs the Matamoros expedition at San Patricio and Agua Dulce
events.detail: Advancing up the coast, Urrea's column surprised Frank Johnson's men at San Patricio on 27 February 1836; six Texians escaped and the rest were killed or captured. On 2 March Mexican dragoons ambushed James Grant's party at Agua Dulce Creek, killing twelve, Grant among them. Both groups were what remained of the planned expedition against Matamoros, which had pulled men and supplies away from San Antonio and Goliad. Urrea's victories opened the coastal road to Goliad.

events.label: 2 Mar 1836
events.text: Texas declares independence at Washington-on-the-Brazos
events.detail: While the Alamo was under siege, an elected convention met at Washington-on-the-Brazos on 1 March 1836. The next day it adopted a declaration of independence proclaiming the Republic of Texas and accusing Santa Anna's government of abandoning the federal constitution. The delegates went on to write a constitution, adopted on 17 March, and chose David G. Burnet as interim president. Sam Houston was confirmed as commander of all Texian forces and left to take charge of the army.

events.label: 6 Mar 1836
events.text: The Alamo falls
events.detail: Before dawn on 6 March 1836 Mexican columns stormed the Alamo from several sides and, after their first attacks were thrown back, broke into the compound. Within about an hour nearly all of the roughly 182 to 257 defenders were dead, including Travis, Bowie and Davy Crockett; a handful who surrendered were executed on Santa Anna's orders. Mexican losses are estimated at 400 to 600 killed and wounded. Susanna Dickinson, her infant daughter and Travis's enslaved servant Joe were spared and sent to Gonzales.

events.label: 13 Mar 1836
events.text: Houston abandons Gonzales and the Runaway Scrape begins
events.detail: Sam Houston had reached Gonzales to gather an army when the survivors of the Alamo brought news of its fall. Around midnight on 13 March 1836 the Texian force evacuated the town, burning whatever it could not carry, and retreated east. Settlers fled ahead of the Mexican advance along flooded rivers and muddy roads, in what became known as the Runaway Scrape. Volunteers kept arriving, and by 19 March about 1,400 men had joined Houston's army.

events.label: 19–20 Mar 1836
events.text: Fannin surrenders after the Battle of Coleto
events.detail: Ordered by Houston to abandon Goliad and fall back, James Fannin delayed and set out only on 19 March 1836. Urrea's troops caught his roughly 300 men on open prairie near Coleto Creek. The Texians held off attacks through the day, losing about nine killed and 51 wounded against some 50 Mexican dead and 140 wounded. Short of water and surrounded, Fannin surrendered on 20 March, believing his men would be treated as prisoners of war, and they were marched back to Goliad.

events.label: 27 Mar 1836
events.text: Goliad massacre: Texian prisoners are executed
events.detail: Fannin's men and other captured Texians were held at Presidio La Bahía. Urrea appealed for clemency, but Santa Anna, citing the decree on foreign volunteers, ordered them executed, and the commander at Goliad, José Nicolás de la Portilla, obeyed. On Palm Sunday, 27 March 1836, the prisoners were marched out and shot: about 350 by the most common count, with some estimates higher. Twenty-eight escaped and others were spared to work as doctors or labourers. 'Remember Goliad' became a Texian rallying cry.

events.label: Mid-Apr 1836
events.text: Santa Anna burns Harrisburg as Houston turns to fight
events.detail: Houston retreated to the Brazos and drilled his army at Groce's Landing before marching east. Santa Anna, hoping to seize the Texian government, pushed ahead with part of his army and reached Harrisburg in mid-April 1836, but the interim government had fled, and he ordered the town burned. Learning on 18 April that Santa Anna's force was small and close by, Houston hurried toward Lynch's Ferry on Buffalo Bayou, arriving on the morning of 20 April.

events.label: 21 Apr 1836
events.text: Battle of San Jacinto: Houston routs Santa Anna
events.detail: Santa Anna camped beside the San Jacinto River, reinforced by Cos to about 1,200–1,360 men. At about 4:30 in the afternoon of 21 April 1836, roughly 900 Texians attacked across open ground shouting 'Remember the Alamo! Remember Goliad!' The Mexican line broke in about 18 minutes, and the killing went on as Texians shot men trying to surrender. About 650 Mexicans were killed and some 300 captured; the Texians lost 11 dead and about 30 wounded, Houston among them.

events.label: 22 Apr 1836
events.text: Santa Anna is captured
events.detail: Santa Anna escaped the battlefield and hid in the marshes, wearing a private's uniform jacket. Texian search parties captured him on 22 April 1836 and brought him before the wounded Houston. Held as a prisoner, he agreed to order the remaining Mexican forces in Texas, under Vicente Filisola and Urrea, to withdraw. Although those armies were still larger than Houston's, they began pulling back toward the Rio Grande.

events.label: 14 May 1836
events.text: Treaties of Velasco: Santa Anna agrees to withdraw
events.detail: At Velasco on 14 May 1836 Santa Anna, still a prisoner, signed two agreements with interim president David G. Burnet. The public treaty ended hostilities and required Mexican troops to withdraw beyond the Rio Grande, exchange prisoners and return captured property, including enslaved people. A secret treaty bound Santa Anna to work for recognition of Texas with a border no farther south than the Rio Grande. Mexico's government disowned both, and did not recognise Texan independence until 1848.

name: Mexican–American War
summary: In 1845 the United States annexed Texas, which had broken away from Mexico in 1836. Mexico had never recognised Texan independence and had threatened war over annexation, and the two countries also disputed the border: Texas claimed the Rio Grande, Mexico the Nueces River farther north. President James K. Polk, who also wanted California and New Mexico, sent John Slidell to buy them and moved Zachary Taylor's army to the Rio Grande. A Mexican attack on a US patrol in the disputed zone on 25 April 1846 led Congress to declare war. Taylor won at Palo Alto, Resaca de la Palma and Monterrey and held off Santa Anna at Buena Vista, while US forces occupied New Mexico and, after a Californio uprising, California. In March 1847 Winfield Scott landed at Veracruz and fought his way inland, taking Mexico City in September. The Treaty of Guadalupe Hidalgo of 1848 gave the United States about 55 percent of Mexico's territory for $15 million, and the fight over slavery in the new lands sharpened the sectional crisis in the United States.
casualties: An estimated 13,000 Americans died, about 1,700 of them killed in battle and most of the rest from disease, while Mexican military and civilian deaths are estimated at up to about 25,000.

sides.name: United States (with the Bear Flag rebels in California, 1846)

events.label: Mar 1846
events.text: Taylor's army advances to the Rio Grande
events.detail: Texas had become the 28th US state on 29 December 1845, and Mexico, which still regarded it as Mexican, had broken off diplomatic relations. Polk's envoy John Slidell, sent with an offer to buy the Rio Grande border, California and New Mexico, was refused. Polk then ordered General Zachary Taylor, camped on the Nueces since 1845, into the disputed land beyond it. In March 1846 Taylor's army reached the Rio Grande opposite Matamoros and began building a fort, later called Fort Texas.

events.label: 25 Apr 1846
events.text: Thornton Affair: Mexican cavalry ambush a US patrol
events.detail: On 23 April 1846 Mexico's president, General Mariano Paredes, declared a defensive war. Two days later a large Mexican cavalry force that had crossed the Rio Grande surrounded a patrol of about 70 US dragoons under Captain Seth Thornton at a ranch upriver from Taylor's fort, killing 11 and capturing 52. Taylor reported to Washington that hostilities had begun, and Polk, who had already been preparing to ask Congress for war, used the clash to argue that Mexico had started it.

events.label: 3 May 1846
events.text: Mexican guns at Matamoros bombard Fort Texas
events.detail: General Mariano Arista crossed the Rio Grande with most of his army, threatening Taylor's supply base at Point Isabel on the coast, and Taylor marched off to secure it. From 3 May 1846 Mexican artillery in Matamoros shelled the fort he had left behind, keeping up the bombardment for some 160 hours. Its commander, Major Jacob Brown, was one of two defenders killed, and the post was renamed Fort Brown in his honour, giving its name to the later city of Brownsville.

events.label: 8 May 1846
events.text: Battle of Palo Alto: US artillery wins the first major battle
events.detail: Returning to relieve the fort, Taylor's roughly 2,300 men met Arista's army of about 3,700 on the coastal prairie of Palo Alto on 8 May 1846. The battle was fought largely with artillery. Mobile US 'flying artillery' batteries fired, moved and fired again, causing heavy losses that the Mexican guns could not match. Mexican casualties were about 102 killed and 129 wounded against nine Americans killed; Major Samuel Ringgold was mortally wounded. That evening Arista pulled back to the south.

events.label: 9 May 1846
events.text: Battle of Resaca de la Palma: Arista's army is routed
events.detail: Arista made a new stand the next day in a dry riverbed, or resaca, lined with thick brush on the road to Matamoros. In close fighting on 9 May 1846 US dragoons captured Mexican artillery, and the Mexican army broke and fled back across the Rio Grande. Fort Texas was relieved. Later in May Taylor crossed the river and occupied Matamoros, which Arista had abandoned, and the war moved south into northern Mexico.

events.label: 13 May 1846
events.text: The United States declares war on Mexico
events.detail: Polk asked Congress for war, arguing that Mexico had begun hostilities on American soil, and Congress approved the declaration on 13 May 1846. Critics, mostly Whigs, accused Polk of provoking the war by sending troops into disputed land; among them, later in the war, was the young congressman Abraham Lincoln, whose 'spot resolutions' challenged Polk to name the spot where the first blood had been shed. Mexico's Congress formally declared war on 7 July 1846.

events.label: 14 Jun 1846
events.text: Bear Flag Revolt: American settlers proclaim a California Republic
events.detail: In Mexico's thinly held province of Alta California, American settlers in the Sacramento Valley, emboldened by the US Army explorer John C. Frémont and his armed party, rose against the Mexican authorities. On 14 June 1846 they seized the barracks at Sonoma and raised a flag bearing a grizzly bear and a star, proclaiming the California Republic under William B. Ide. It lasted 25 days: on 9 July the US flag was raised at Sonoma, and the rebels joined Frémont's California Battalion.

events.label: 7 Jul 1846
events.text: US Navy takes Monterey, capital of Alta California
events.detail: Commodore John D. Sloat's Pacific Squadron landed sailors and marines at Monterey, the capital of Alta California, on 7 July 1846 and took the town without a shot. Two days later another landing party took Yerba Buena, the future San Francisco. Commodore Robert Stockton, who succeeded Sloat, joined forces with Frémont, and on 13 August 1846 US troops entered Los Angeles unopposed. Within weeks of the first landings, California seemed to be won.

events.label: Aug 1846
events.text: Mexico restores its federal constitution and Santa Anna returns
events.detail: The defeats on the Rio Grande discredited the centralist government of Paredes, who was overthrown in the summer of 1846. Federalist liberals restored the Constitution of 1824, and José Mariano Salas became acting president. Santa Anna, in exile in Cuba, returned in August after the US Navy let him through its blockade of the Gulf coast, in the belief that he would make peace. Instead he took command of the army and raised a new force at San Luis Potosí.

events.label: 18 Aug 1846
events.text: Kearny occupies Santa Fe and New Mexico without a fight
events.detail: General Stephen W. Kearny led the Army of the West, about 1,600 regulars and volunteers, from Fort Leavenworth down the Santa Fe Trail. Governor Manuel Armijo gathered militia at Apache Canyon east of Santa Fe, then withdrew without fighting and fled south to Chihuahua. Kearny entered Santa Fe and on 18 August 1846 took possession of New Mexico, declaring himself military governor and setting up a civil government. Leaving a garrison behind, he set out for California the following month.

events.label: 20–24 Sep 1846
events.text: Battle of Monterrey
events.detail: Taylor advanced on Monterrey, a fortified city in Nuevo León held by General Pedro de Ampudia. From 20 September 1846 his troops attacked the forts on the city's outskirts and then fought their way street by street into the centre, taking heavy losses. On 24 September Ampudia agreed to give up Monterrey in return for an eight-week armistice and the free withdrawal of his army. Polk disliked the terms, and Taylor later ended the truce by occupying Saltillo.

events.label: Late Sep 1846
events.text: Californios rise and retake Los Angeles
events.detail: The small US garrison left in Los Angeles under Archibald Gillespie imposed strict rules that angered the Californios, the Mexican residents of the province. In late September 1846 they rose under José María Flores and forced the garrison to withdraw, and the revolt spread across southern California, where Mexican control was restored for the rest of the year. US forces could not retake the city that autumn, and the conquest of California had to be fought again.

events.label: 6 Dec 1846
events.text: Battle of San Pasqual: Californio lancers defeat Kearny
events.detail: Kearny reached southern California after a hard march across the desert with a small force of dragoons. On 6 December 1846, near the village of San Pasqual, about 150 Americans attacked some 100 Californio lancers under Andrés Pico. The lancers, expert horsemen, turned on the scattered American column and cut it up in about half an hour; 22 Americans were killed and Kearny himself was wounded. Pinned on a hilltop, his force was rescued by sailors and marines sent from San Diego.

events.label: 8–13 Jan 1847
events.text: Los Angeles is retaken and the Californios capitulate at Cahuenga
events.detail: Stockton and Kearny marched north from San Diego with a combined force of sailors, marines and soldiers. They defeated Flores's Californios at the Río San Gabriel on 8 January 1847 and at La Mesa the next day, and entered Los Angeles unopposed on 10 January. On 13 January Andrés Pico and John C. Frémont signed the Articles of Capitulation at Cahuenga Pass, which allowed the Californios to go home and ended the fighting in California.

events.label: 19 Jan 1847
events.text: Taos Revolt against the US occupation of New Mexico
events.detail: Many New Mexicans resented the American occupation. On 19 January 1847 Hispano and Pueblo insurgents at Taos killed the new governor, Charles Bent, and other officials, and the next day attacked Turley's mill at Arroyo Hondo. Colonel Sterling Price marched north from Santa Fe with more than 300 soldiers and volunteers and besieged the rebels in Taos Pueblo in early February. About 150 rebels were killed and some 400 captured, against seven Americans dead, and the revolt was crushed.

events.label: 22–23 Feb 1847
events.text: Battle of Buena Vista: Taylor holds off Santa Anna
events.detail: Many of Taylor's regulars had been sent to join Winfield Scott's planned landing at Veracruz. Santa Anna marched north from San Luis Potosí, losing thousands of men on the way, and on 22–23 February 1847 attacked Taylor's roughly 4,600 men, mostly volunteers, at the pass of La Angostura near the Buena Vista hacienda south of Saltillo. His army of about 15,000 came close to breaking the US line. Both sides claimed victory, but Santa Anna withdrew, and the battle made Taylor a national hero.

events.label: 9–29 Mar 1847
events.text: Scott lands at Veracruz and takes the city
events.detail: Polk decided to strike at Mexico City from the sea. On 9 March 1847 Winfield Scott put his army ashore on the beaches south of Veracruz without opposition, the first major amphibious landing in US history. His troops surrounded the walled port, and from 22 March siege and naval guns bombarded it, killing hundreds of civilians. The defenders asked for terms on 26 March, and on 29 March the city and the island fortress of San Juan de Ulúa surrendered, with some 3,000 soldiers taken prisoner.

events.label: 18 Apr 1847
events.text: Battle of Cerro Gordo: Scott breaks through to the highlands
events.detail: Scott marched inland along the National Road, eager to leave the coast before the yellow-fever season. Santa Anna blocked the road at the mountain pass of Cerro Gordo with a large army in strong positions. Scouts, among them Captain Robert E. Lee, found a path around the Mexican left, and on 18 April 1847 Scott's army of about 8,500 attacked from flank and front. The Mexican army collapsed, losing more than 1,000 killed and wounded and about 3,000 prisoners, against some 400 US casualties.

events.label: 19–20 Aug 1847
events.text: Battles of Contreras and Churubusco outside Mexico City
events.detail: After waiting months at Puebla for reinforcements, Scott advanced on Mexico City in August 1847. On 19–20 August his army routed a Mexican force at Contreras (Padierna) and then stormed the fortified convent of Churubusco, defended to the last by Mexican troops and the Saint Patrick's Battalion, made up mostly of Irish and other immigrant deserters from the US Army. US losses at Churubusco were more than 1,000 killed, wounded and missing. An armistice followed, but peace talks broke down on 6 September.

events.label: 8 Sep 1847
events.text: Battle of Molino del Rey
events.detail: When the armistice ended, Scott sent William Worth's division against Molino del Rey, a group of stone mill buildings about a thousand yards west of the hill of Chapultepec, where he believed cannon were being cast. Mexican troops put up a fierce defence on 8 September 1847, and the Americans took the buildings only at heavy cost to both sides. Scott then turned on Chapultepec Castle, the hilltop fortress and military college that guarded the western approaches to the capital.

events.label: 13 Sep 1847
events.text: Storming of Chapultepec Castle
events.detail: After a bombardment that began on 12 September, US troops stormed Chapultepec Castle on the morning of 13 September 1847 and took it by about 9 a.m. Among its roughly 830 defenders were cadets of the military college; six who died there are honoured in Mexico as the Niños Héroes. Nearby, thirty captured members of the Saint Patrick's Battalion were hanged at the moment the US flag replaced the Mexican one over the castle. US troops then fought their way to the city gates of Belén and San Cosme.

events.label: 14 Sep 1847
events.text: US troops occupy Mexico City
events.detail: Santa Anna withdrew his remaining troops from the capital during the night, and on 14 September 1847 Scott's army marched into Mexico City and raised the US flag over the National Palace. Scott became military governor of the occupied city. Santa Anna soon gave up the presidency, and a new Mexican government gathered at Querétaro, while guerrillas attacked US supply lines between the capital and the coast. Fighting dwindled, but peace still had to be negotiated.

events.label: 9 Oct 1847
events.text: Battle of Huamantla: Santa Anna's last battle
events.detail: Santa Anna made a final attempt to cut Scott's communications by besieging the US garrison left at Puebla. A relief column under General Joseph Lane, marching inland from Veracruz, defeated his troops at Huamantla on 9 October 1847, after which Lane's men sacked the town. Puebla was relieved on 12 October. It was the last battle Santa Anna fought in the war, and the remaining Mexican resistance was left to guerrilla bands.

events.label: 2 Feb 1848
events.text: Treaty of Guadalupe Hidalgo ends the war
events.detail: The US envoy Nicholas Trist, ignoring Polk's order recalling him, negotiated with Mexico's government, and on 2 February 1848 a treaty was signed at Guadalupe Hidalgo, just north of Mexico City. Mexico gave up all claims to Texas, with the border on the Rio Grande, and ceded about 55 percent of its territory: present-day California, Nevada, Utah, New Mexico, most of Arizona and parts of several other states. The United States paid $15 million and assumed up to $3.25 million in its citizens' claims against Mexico.

events.label: 10 Mar 1848
events.text: The US Senate ratifies the treaty
events.detail: Polk, angry with Trist but content with the terms, sent the treaty to the Senate, where some members wanted to annex more of Mexico and others wanted no territory at all. The Senate approved it on 10 March 1848 by 38 votes to 14, after deleting Article X, which protected Mexican land grants. Formal hostilities had ended on 6 March. The war left a bitter question behind: the Wilmot Proviso, which would have barred slavery from the new lands, had passed the House in 1847 but failed in the Senate.

events.label: 30 May 1848
events.text: Ratifications exchanged at Querétaro; US troops withdraw
events.detail: Mexico's Congress, meeting at Querétaro, debated the amended treaty and approved it in May 1848. Ratifications were exchanged there on 30 May, and the treaty was proclaimed in the United States on 4 July. US troops left Mexico City in June and had evacuated Mexico by August. Mexicans living in the ceded lands could stay and keep their property; those who did not choose Mexican citizenship within a year would become citizens of the United States.
